title: find, cut, tr, sort, uniq and xargs pipelines
goal: Find files by name, age and size, act on them safely, and build classic one-line pipelines like "top 10 IPs".
setup: # P1/P2 use srv/, P5 uses night/srv/ (the same files, so the problems do not change each other)
for s in srv night/srv; do
for i in 1 2 3; do echo "log line $i" > "$s/app/app-$i.log"; done
# P3: an access log with 12 client IPs (fixed counts)
printf '%s\n' 'a3f9c1e7d2b4 fix login bug' '9b1d77e0aa31 add health endpoint' > commits.txt
# P5: two .log files in night/ (they make an unquoted *.log expand) and a broken cleanup script
echo x > night/cleanup.log; echo y > night/run.log

printf '%s\n' '#!/bin/bash' '# 1) list .log files under srv/ that are older than 7 days' '# 2) show the 3 biggest files under srv/ (size in bytes, biggest first)' '# 3) delete the .tmp files in srv/tmp (names may contain spaces)' 'find srv -name *.log -mtime 7' "find srv -type f -printf '%s %p\\n' | sort | head -n 3" "find srv/tmp -name '*.tmp' | xargs rm" > night/cleanup.sh
# P6: a disk report with human sizes

warmup.q: Which sed command prints only lines 5 to 8?
How do you print the first column of a CSV with awk?

warmup.a: Only the names of the files under `configs/` that contain `db01`.

warmup.q: Which loop is safe for file names with spaces: `for f in $(ls)` or `for f in *`?

problems.title: find files by name, type, age and size
problems.situation: The research server's disk is almost full. Before deleting anything, the user must list: all log files, logs older than 7 days, big files over 10 MB, and old folders. The files are under `srv/`.
task: List all regular files ending in `.log` under `srv` (`-type f -name`).
List files modified more than 7 days ago (`-mtime +7`).
List files bigger than 10 MB (`-size +10M`).
Combine: `.log` files that are older than 7 days.
List folders (`-type d`) that were not changed for more than 20 days. Add `| sort` to every command so the order is stable.
hints: Always quote the pattern: `-name '*.log'`, or bash expands it first.
`-mtime +7` = more than 7 full days ago. `-mtime -2` = less than 2 days ago.
Size units: `k`, `M`, `G`. `+10M` = more than 10 MB.

explanation.meaning: Start searching in `srv` and go into every sub-folder.
Only regular files / only folders (directories).
Name pattern. Quote it so find gets the `*`, not bash.
Modified more than 7 days ago (in whole days).
Bigger than 10 MB. `-size -1k` would be smaller than 1 KB.
Several tests mean AND: every test must be true. Use `-o` for OR.

problems.expected_output:
srv/app/app-1.log
srv/app/app-2.log
srv/app/app-3.log
srv/nginx/access.log
=== older than 7 days ===
srv/app/app-2.log
srv/app/app-3.log
srv/nginx/access.log.1
=== bigger than 10 MB ===
srv/app/heap-dump.hprof
srv/nginx/access.log.1
=== .log and older than 7 days ===
srv/app/app-2.log
srv/app/app-3.log
=== old folders ===
srv/app/old-builds
problems.output_note: `access.log.1` and `heap-dump.hprof` are sparse files: they report a big size but use almost no disk space. They are safe practice files.
mistakes: `find srv -name *.log` without quotes: if the current folder has .log files, bash expands the pattern and find gets the wrong arguments (see P5).
`-mtime 7` (no plus) means exactly 7 days old, which is usually not what the user wants.
Putting the path last: `find -name '*.log' srv` gives the error `find: paths must precede expression`, and it names `srv`.
problems.interview_say: I use `find PATH -type f -name '*.log' -mtime +7 -size +10M` to list files by name, age and size. I always quote the name pattern, and I list before I delete.
problems.try_yourself: Find files changed in the last 60 minutes: `find srv -mmin -60`. Then `touch srv/app/app-1.log` and run it again.

problems.title: find -exec and -delete, safely
problems.situation: Now the user acts on the files: delete old temp files, and compress logs older than 7 days. A wrong `find -delete` can remove the wrong files, so the user always runs the same command with `-print` first.
task: Dry run: list `.tmp` files in `srv/tmp` older than 3 days with `-print`.
Run the same command with `-delete` instead. List `srv/tmp` after.
Compress `.log` files older than 7 days with `-exec gzip -v {} \;`.
List the `.gz` files that now exist.
hints: Same command, two steps: first `-print`, then `-delete`. Change nothing else.
`{}` is replaced by each file name. `\;` ends the `-exec` command (one run per file).
`-exec cmd {} +` runs `cmd` once with many files: faster.
solution: find srv/tmp -type f -name '*.tmp' -mtime +3 -print | sort      # 1. dry run
find srv/tmp -type f -name '*.tmp' -mtime +3 -delete            # 2. same test, delete

explanation.meaning: See exactly which files match. Only then use `-delete`.
Delete every match. Put it last, after all tests.
Run `gzip -v FILE` for each match. `\;` = end of the command.
Compress and replace the file with `.gz`; `-v` prints the result.
Pass many files at once: `gzip a b c` instead of 3 runs.

problems.expected_output:
srv/tmp/a.tmp
srv/tmp/b.tmp
srv/tmp/my file.tmp
keep.conf
srv/app/app-3.log:	-18.2% -- replaced with srv/app/app-3.log.gz
srv/app/app-2.log:	-18.2% -- replaced with srv/app/app-2.log.gz
srv/app/app-2.log.gz
srv/app/app-3.log.gz
problems.output_note: `find` lists files in the order of the folder on disk, so the two gzip lines can be in a different order on the user's machine.
mistakes: Putting `-delete` first: `find srv -delete -name '*.tmp'` deletes **everything** under srv before testing the name.
Forgetting `\;` or `+`: find stops with `find: missing argument to` and names `-exec`.
Deleting logs that a program still writes to. Compress old rotated logs only; for live logs use logrotate (Day 16).
problems.interview_say: Before `find -delete` I run the same command with `-print`. I put `-delete` at the end. For other actions I use `-exec cmd {} +` to run the command on many files at once.
problems.try_yourself: Compress with the `+` form and see the difference: `find srv -name '*.log' -exec ls -l {} +`.

problems.title: The classic: top 10 client IPs
problems.situation: The API gets many requests and the team suspects one client is flooding it. The interviewer's favourite one-liner: show the 10 IP addresses with the most requests in the access log, with counts.
task: Print the first field (IP) of each line.
Sort the IPs so equal ones are together, and count them with `uniq -c`.
Sort the counts as numbers, biggest first (`sort -rn`).
Keep the first 10 lines.
Do the same with `cut -d' ' -f1` instead of awk. Then show only the top 1 IP.
hints: `awk '{print $1}' access.log`
`... | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 10`
`-n` = numeric sort, `-r` = reverse (biggest first).
solution: awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 10
cut -d' ' -f1 access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 1
echo "=== total requests and unique IPs ==="

explanation.meaning: Take the IP (first field).
Put equal IPs next to each other, so uniq can count them.
Count each group: `31 10.0.0.5`.
Sort by the number, biggest first. Without `-n`, `9` comes after `31` (text order).
Keep the top 10.
Same as awk here: field 1, with space as delimiter.

mistakes: Forgetting the first `sort`: `uniq -c` counts only neighbours, so one IP appears many times.
`sort -r` without `-n`: text order puts `9` before `31`, because `9` > `3`.
problems.interview_say: `awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head` gives the top IPs. The first sort groups equal lines, uniq counts them, and `sort -rn` puts the biggest count first.
problems.try_yourself: Show the top status codes instead: which field number is the status code in this log format?

problems.title: Reshape text: cut, tr and paste
problems.situation: Small reshaping jobs: take user names and home folders from a passwd-style file, short git commit ids, fix a host list that came from Windows (with hidden `\r` characters), and join two lists side by side.
task: From `users.db` (separated by `:`), print fields 1 and 6.
From `commits.txt`, print the first 7 characters of each line (short SHA).
Show the hidden characters of `hosts-windows.txt` with `cat -A`. Remove the `\r` with `tr -d '\r'`.
Change `hosts.txt` to upper case with `tr`, and squeeze repeated spaces with `tr -s ' '`.
Join `hosts.txt` and `ips.txt` side by side with `paste`, and join all hosts into one line with commas (`paste -sd,`).
hints: `cut -d: -f1,6` = delimiter `:`, fields 1 and 6. `cut -c1-7` = characters 1 to 7.
`cat -A` shows `^M` for `\r` and `$` at each line end.
`tr 'a-z' 'A-Z'` maps lower to upper. `paste -sd, file` = serial, delimiter comma.

explanation.meaning: Split at `:` and keep fields 1 and 6 (user and home).
Keep characters 1 to 7.
Show hidden characters: `^M` = Windows `\r`, `$` = end of line.
Delete every `\r`. Fixes files edited on Windows (`$'\r': command not found` in scripts).
Map characters / squeeze repeats into one.
Join lines side by side (TAB between) / join all lines of one file with commas.

problems.expected_output:
root:/root
wicky:/home/wicky
jenkins:/var/lib/jenkins
nginx:/var/www
a3f9c1e
9b1d77e
web-01^M$
web-02^M$
web-01$
web-02$
WEB-01
WEB-02
DB-01
too many spaces
web-01	10.0.1.10
web-02	10.0.1.11
db-01	10.0.2.20
web-01,web-02,db-01
mistakes: `tr` does not take a file name: `tr 'a-z' 'A-Z' hosts.txt` gives `tr: extra operand ‘hosts.txt’`. Use `< hosts.txt`.
A script written in Windows Notepad fails with `$'\r': command not found`. Fix it with `tr -d '\r'` or `dos2unix`.
`cut` with spaces: many spaces in a row create empty fields. Use `tr -s ' '` first, or `awk`.
problems.interview_say: `cut` takes fields or characters, `tr` translates or deletes characters, and `paste` joins lines. `tr -d '\r'` is my fix for files that came from Windows.
problems.try_yourself: Run `cut -d: -f7 users.db | sort | uniq -c`. How many users have each shell?

problems.title: Find the bug: the cleanup script
problems.situation: `cleanup.sh` runs every night. It prints a strange find error, shows the wrong "biggest" files, and fails to delete one temp file. The goals are in the comments.
task: Run `bash cleanup.sh` and read every error line.
Find 4 bugs: an unquoted pattern, a wrong `-mtime`, a wrong sort, and xargs with spaces.
Fix them and run again. The biggest file must be `heap-dump.hprof`, and `srv/tmp` must keep only `keep.conf`.
hints: There are two `.log` files in `night/`, so `*.log` becomes `cleanup.log run.log`.
`-mtime 7` = exactly 7 days. Use `+7`. Sizes are numbers: `sort -rn`.
Use `find ... -delete`, or `-print0 | xargs -0 rm`, for names with spaces.
solution: # 1) list .log files under srv/ that are older than 7 days
# 2) show the 3 biggest files under srv/ (size in bytes, biggest first)
# 3) delete the .tmp files in srv/tmp (names may contain spaces)

explanation.meaning: Bug 1: unquoted, bash expanded it to `cleanup.log run.log`: `paths must precede expression`.
Bug 2: `7` = exactly 7 days; `+7` = more than 7 days.
Bug 3: plain `sort` is text order and smallest first. Sizes need numeric, reverse.
Bug 4: `my file.tmp` was split into `my` and `file.tmp`. Null-separated names are safe.
GNU find: print size in bytes and path.

problems.expected_output:
find: paths must precede expression: `run.log'
find: possible unquoted pattern after predicate `-name'?
0 srv/tmp/a.tmp
0 srv/tmp/b.tmp
0 srv/tmp/keep.conf
rm: cannot remove 'srv/tmp/my': No such file or directory
rm: cannot remove 'file.tmp': No such file or directory
--- fixed ---
srv/app/app-2.log
srv/app/app-3.log
125829120 srv/app/heap-dump.hprof
15728640 srv/nginx/access.log.1
11 srv/app/app-3.log
removed 'srv/tmp/my file.tmp'
keep.conf
mistakes: Running the broken script in a folder without `.log` files: bug 1 hides, because the pattern is not expanded there. It breaks only in some folders.
Using `ls -S` for the biggest files: it does not search sub-folders. `find -printf` or `du` (Day 17) does.

checks.expect: rm: cannot remove 'srv/tmp/my': No such file or directory

problems.interview_say: In cleanup scripts I quote find patterns, use `-mtime +N`, sort sizes with `sort -rn`, and use `-delete` or `-print0 | xargs -0` so names with spaces are safe.
problems.try_yourself: Run `cd srv && find . -name *.log` (no quotes) inside `srv`, where no .log file is in the top folder. Why does it work there?

problems.title: sort by a column: -k -t -h -u
problems.situation: `du -h` style reports show sizes like `800M`, `1.5G`, `12G`. Sorting them as text or as plain numbers gives the wrong order. `sort -h` understands human sizes, and `-k` picks the column.
task: Sort `disk.txt` by the second column as text: `sort -k2`.
Sort it with `-n`. Is it right?
Sort it with `-h` (human numbers), biggest first.
Sort `users.db` by the user id (field 3, separator `:`) as numbers.
hints: `-k2` = sort by column 2 (to the end of the line). `-k2,2` = only column 2.
`-h` knows that `1.5G` > `800M`.
`-t:` sets the separator: `sort -t: -k3,3 -n users.db`.

explanation.meaning: Use column 2 as the sort key.
Numeric, but it ignores units: `12G` is smaller than `40K` because 12 < 40.
Human-readable numbers: K < M < G.
Separator `:`, key is field 3 only.

problems.expected_output:
logs 1.5G
docker 12G
jenkins 3.2G
tmp 40K
home 800M
=== -n (wrong for units) ===
logs 1.5G
jenkins 3.2G
docker 12G
tmp 40K
home 800M
=== -h, biggest first ===
docker 12G
jenkins 3.2G
logs 1.5G
home 800M
tmp 40K
=== users by id ===
root:0
nginx:997
jenkins:998
wicky:1000
mistakes: Using `-k3` instead of `-k3,3`: the key runs to the end of the line, which can change ties.
problems.interview_say: `sort -k` picks a column, `-t` sets the separator, `-n` sorts numbers, and `-h` sorts human sizes like `du -h` output. `du -sh * | sort -h` shows the biggest folders last.
problems.try_yourself: Run `sort -u -t: -k7,7 users.db | cut -d: -f7`. What does `-u` with a key do?

problems.title: xargs -n and -P: checks in parallel
problems.situation: A health check takes 1 second per server. For 4 servers that is 4 seconds one by one. `xargs -P` runs several at the same time. Here a `sleep 1` is the fake check, so it is safe to run.
task: Run the fake check `./check.sh HOST` for 4 hosts one by one with `xargs -n 1`, and measure the time with `SECONDS`.
Run them with `-P 4` (4 at the same time) and measure again.
Sort the parallel output: the order of finished jobs can change every run.
hints: `SECONDS` is a bash variable: seconds since the shell started. Set it to 0 first.
`printf '%s\n' web-01 web-02 web-03 web-04 | xargs -n 1 -P 4 ./check.sh`
Parallel output order is not fixed, so add `| sort`.
solution: printf '%s\n' web-01 web-02 web-03 web-04 | xargs -n 1 ./check.sh
printf '%s\n' web-01 web-02 web-03 web-04 | xargs -n 1 -P 4 ./check.sh | sort

explanation.meaning: One argument per command run.
Up to 4 commands at the same time.
The fake check: it sleeps 1 second and prints `HOST ok`.
Bash counts seconds; set it to 0 to start a stopwatch.

problems.expected_output:
web-01 ok
web-02 ok
web-03 ok
web-04 ok
web-01 ok
web-02 ok
web-03 ok
web-04 ok
one by one: 5s, parallel: 1s
parallel is faster
problems.output_note: The seconds can be a little different. The parallel run should take about 1 second instead of about 4.
mistakes: Using `-P` with commands that write to the same file: the lines can mix. Write to separate files or use `| sort`.
Using a very big `-P` against a production API: it looks like an attack. Keep it small.
problems.interview_say: `xargs -P N` runs up to N commands in parallel, which is useful for checks on many servers. I sort the output because the order of finished jobs is not fixed.
problems.try_yourself: Try `-P 2`. How many seconds does it take now?

interview.q: How do you find log files bigger than 100 MB and older than 30 days?
How do you safely delete files found by find?
interview.a: Run the command with `-print` first to check the list, then the same command with `-delete` at the end. For names with spaces use `-print0 | xargs -0`.

interview.q: How do you get the top 10 IP addresses from an access log?

interview.a: Files with Windows line endings. The `\r` makes scripts fail with `$'\r': command not found`.

interview.q: What is the difference between `-exec cmd {} \;` and `-exec cmd {} +`?
interview.a: `\;` runs the command once per file. `+` runs it once with many files, which is faster.

recap.meaning: Older than N days / newer than N minutes
Run a command per file / for many files
Join files side by side / lines into one
